bottom_line: In patients with left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction, captopril vs placebo reduced mortality from all causes by 19 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 3 to 32 percent; P = 0.019).
implications: Based on the reported event rates, this trial supports that, in this enrolled population, captopril was associated with lower all-cause mortality (19 percent risk reduction; 95 percent confidence interval, 3 to 32 percent) and lower risks of several major cardiovascular outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular death 21 percent; severe heart failure 37 percent; recurrent myocardial infarction 25 percent). The document also reports more frequent symptoms such as cough with captopril and higher discontinuation due to cough (27 vs 9). These numbers do not establish benefit or safety in patients outside the studied post–myocardial infarction group with ejection fraction of 40 percent or less and without overt heart failure or ischemic symptoms as enrolled here.

major_points.text: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 2231 post–myocardial infarction patients with left ventricular dysfunction.
major_points.quote:
The trial was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
trial in 2231 patients with an acute myocardial infarction and
left ventricular dysfunction

major_points.text: Patients were randomized within 3 to 16 days after myocardial infarction, with ejection fraction ≤40% and without overt heart failure or symptoms of myocardial ischemia.
major_points.quote:
Within 3 to 16 days after myocardial infarc-
tion, 2231 patients with ejection fractions of 40 percent or
less but without overt heart failure or symptoms of myocar-
dial ischemia

were followed for an average of
42 months.

major_points.text: All-cause mortality was 20% with captopril vs 25% with placebo; risk reduction 19% (95% CI 3 to 32).
major_points.quote:
There were 503 deaths during the study: 275 of the
1116 patients (25 percent) in the placebo group and
228 of 1115 (20 percent) in the captopril group; the
reduction in the risk of death from all causes was 19
percent (95 percent confidence interval, 3 to 32 per-
cent; P = 0.019)

major_points.text: Cardiovascular mortality risk was reduced by 21% (95% CI 5 to 35).
major_points.quote:
Of the deaths, 84 percent (422 of 503) were due to
cardiovascular causes (234 in the placebo group vs.
188 in the captopril group); the reduction in risk was
21 percent (95 percent confidence interval, 5 to 35
percent; P = 0.014)

major_points.text: Severe heart failure requiring open-label ACE inhibitor therapy was reduced (11% vs 16%); risk reduction 37% (95% CI 20 to 50).
major_points.quote:
the patients randomly assigned
to receive captopril were significantly less likely to
have this form of treatment failure than those assigned
to placebo (118 of 1115 [11 percent] vs. 179 of 1116
[16 percent], respectively; reduction in risk, 37 per-
cent; 95 percent confidence interval, 20 to 50 percent;
P<0.001)

major_points.text: Congestive heart failure requiring hospitalization was reduced (14% vs 17%); risk reduction 22% (95% CI 4 to 37).
major_points.quote:
the proportion of patients
who required hospitalization for congestive heart fail-
ure was reduced (to 14 percent, or 154 of 1115 pa-
tients, vs. 17 percent, or 192 of 1116 patients, with
placebo; risk reduction, 22 percent; 95 percent confi-
dence interval, 4 to 37 percent; P = 0.019)

major_points.text: Recurrent (fatal or nonfatal) myocardial infarction was reduced; risk reduction 25% (95% CI 5 to 40).
major_points.quote:
After randomization, 303 patients had at least one
clinically reported (fatal or nonfatal) myocardial in-
farction (170 patients in the placebo group and 133
in the captopril group; reduction in risk, 25 per-
cent; 95 percent confidence interval, 5 to 40 percent;
P = 0.015)
